title: the abduction
hook: carried into the sky, Sita turns the whole forest into witnesses

segments.voice: Yesterday: a holy man at the door, a seat and water, and then a name, Ravana. Sita answered him: a lion and a jackal.

Words didn't stop him. Valmiki says Ravana's face changes, his eyes go red, and the holy man's body falls away like a costume. In its place stands the king of Lanka, huge and dark as a storm cloud. He seizes Sita, and his chariot, waiting out of sight, rises into the sky. Below, the hut gets smaller and smaller. Then Sita does something unexpected. She starts talking to the forest.
screen: `THE COSTUME FALLS AWAY.` → `A CHARIOT RISES.` → `SHE TALKS TO THE FOREST.`

segments.voice: Listen to who she calls. Rama, of course, and Lakshmana, the brother she drove away with cruel words; Valmiki doesn't stop to settle that, he lets it hang. Then she turns to everything around her: the flowering trees of Janasthana, the Godavari river, the spirits of the forest, the deer, the birds, anything alive that will still be there when Rama comes back. Tell him Ravana has taken Sita. It sounds like panic, and partly it is. But it's also a plan. Rama will come back to an empty hut with nobody human there to explain, so she makes the whole forest her witnesses. And she names him. Not just a demon took me, but Ravana. The message carries who, not only what. Later in the flight, Valmiki pulls the view wide: the river, the trees, the animals running beneath the chariot's shadow, and Sita in yellow silk against Ravana's dark shape, like lightning against a cloud. This isn't only a household's disaster; the poem wants the whole world to see it. But first, in a tall tree, Sita sees a bird she knows: an old vulture, half asleep in the branches. She calls his name.
screen: `SHE CALLS RAMA, AND LAKSHMANA.` · `THE TREES, THE RIVER, THE DEER.` · `A NAME IN THE MESSAGE: RAVANA.` · `LIGHTNING AGAINST A CLOUD.`

segments.voice: Look around and pick three things that have been there all day: a tree outside, a wall, a cup. Let them be your witnesses while you breathe slowly, with nothing to report and nothing to fix. When your mind runs off, come back to the three things; you are not unseen.
The abduction. Ravana drops the disguise, and Sita, carried into the sky, turns the forest into witnesses.
Your line: like lightning against a cloud. Up in a tall tree, an old friend wakes. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Ramlila performances stage the abduction, and tellings that follow Valmiki keep Sita's cries to the forest and its creatures.

fork.setup: you're Sita, carried into the sky. nobody human is below. what do you do?
options: stay silent and save your strength.
call to the trees, the river and the animals to tell Rama.
plead with Ravana to turn back.
fork.reveal: she calls on the whole forest, by name, to carry the message: Ravana has taken Sita.

original.note: Sanskrit sītāharaṇa: the carrying-off of Sita. a common name for this episode in tellings and plays.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sita just screams for help.
what it means: she turns the forest into witnesses and names her abductor.
what a scholar hears: Aranya 49 has Sita address the trees of Janasthana, the Godavari and the forest beings; the lightning-and-cloud image recurs in the chariot scenes.

chat.says: When Ravana carried Sita off, why did she call out to trees and rivers?
options: With no one human there, she made the forest her witnesses, so Rama would learn who took her.
She believed the trees and rivers had the power to fight Ravana and pull her back down.
She was too frightened to think, and was only calling out whatever she could see.
chat.meaning: Sita knew Rama would come back to an empty hut, so she asked the trees, the river and the animals to tell him: Ravana has taken Sita.

Janasthana.meaning: the forest region around Panchavati, once Khara's

Lanka.meaning: Ravana's island kingdom across the sea

Ravana.meaning: the king of Lanka, who carries Sita off

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda 49 (Ravana takes his own form; Sita calls to the forest)
Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda 52 (Sita in the sky, like lightning against a cloud)

notes: Sarga numbers follow the common (vulgate) numbering and differ between editions; confirm against the edition the Keeper uses.
Ravana's change of form (red eyes, huge size) paraphrased; Valmiki's description of heads and arms here varies by edition, so the script says only 'huge and dark'.
The lightning-against-a-cloud image and Sita's yellow silk: confirm sarga (49 or 52).
'Ramlila performances often stage...' in howItsDone is a general description; a Keeper may wish to adjust.
